name: Study.com
line: Study.com teaches math in video lessons, in a set order. In AMP, the problem is the unit and every answer sets the next.
description: AMP vs Study.com: Study.com teaches math in video lessons and quizzes, in a set order. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous.
verdict: Study.com teaches math in courses of video lessons, each followed by a short quiz, in a set order the parent paces [1][2]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous: every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Study.com describes no placement test. The parent or learner picks a course at any grade, and the course runs in a set order of chapters and lessons, with a quiz after each lesson and a test after each chapter [1][2].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Study.com the unit is the video lesson: a video of about five minutes, with a transcript and flashcards, then a short quiz [1][2]. Its FAQ says the vast majority of homeschool lessons are video lessons [2]. In an online psychology course for adults, students who did more interactive activities learned more than students who watched more video or read more pages. The data are correlational [7].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After each answer AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. Study.com's FAQ says a lesson quiz can be retaken with the same questions [2]. We found no hints or worked steps for a missed quiz question in the pages we read [2]. Across 40 studies of computer feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect [8].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a learner shows a skill by getting it right without help, more than once, and moves on. An answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Study.com states no mastery rule. Scores are not averaged across tests, and the parent decides which ones count [2]. We found no automatic return to earlier skills in the pages we read [2].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. A Study.com course moves forward chapter by chapter, with a test at the end of each [2][3]. We found no scheduled review of earlier lessons in the pages we read [2][3]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [9].

reasons.title: The adult's part
reasons.body: In AMP the adult does not plan, teach or grade. AMP places the learner, chooses each problem, checks it and schedules review. The adult sees a level for each part of math and the actual problems behind every number. On Study.com the parent sets the pace, decides each day's work, grades the optional assignments and sets the final course grade [2].

rows.range: Grade 3 math through Precalculus, plus Statistics 101, in separate courses [1][4].
rows.start: The parent or learner picks a course at any grade. We found no placement test [1][2].
rows.teaching: Video lessons of about five minutes, with transcripts and flashcards. Expert instructors answer questions at any hour [1][2].
rows.next: The course's set order of chapters and lessons, or a custom course the parent builds from chosen lessons [2].
rows.mastery: No stated rule. Lesson quizzes retake with the same questions, chapter tests with new ones. The parent decides which scores count [2].
rows.review: A test at the end of each chapter. We found no scheduled review of earlier lessons [2][3].
rows.print: Printable lesson transcripts. 6th Grade Math includes a chapter of lesson plans [2][3].
rows.adult: Sets the pace, plans daily work, grades optional assignments and sets the final course grade [2].
rows.reports: Each student's progress, a downloadable gradebook of quiz scores, and weekly progress reports [2].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [5][6].

theirs: Study.com makes online video courses, test prep and college-credit courses. Its homeschool edition covers every subject from grade 3 to 12 [1][2]. In math it has courses for grades 3 through 8, Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II, Precalculus and Statistics 101 [1].

A family picks a course, and the course runs in a set order of chapters and lessons [2]. Most lessons are a video of about five minutes, with a transcript and flashcards, and a short quiz ends each one. A test ends each chapter [1][2]. The parent sets the pace and the daily work, and can build a custom course from chosen lessons [2]. Expert instructors answer questions at any hour [1].
credit: Short video lessons with transcripts, captions and flashcards [1][2].
A person to ask. Expert instructors answer questions at any hour [1].
Chapter tests can be retaken with new questions [2].

theirs: We found no outcome study of Study.com on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [5][6].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. In an online psychology course for adults, students who did more interactive activities learned more than students who watched more video or read more pages; the authors estimate the benefit of extra doing at more than six times that of extra watching or reading, and the data are correlational [7]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, practice that mixed and spaced topics scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [9]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: Your child learns well from a short video lesson before practice, with a person to ask at any hour.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want every answer followed by the correct answer and the worked steps.
You want the program, not you, to choose each problem and check it.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Study.com?
questions.answer: Study.com teaches math in video lessons, each followed by a short quiz, in a set order the parent paces [1][2]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Study.com work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of Study.com on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [5][6].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. A learner can use Study.com for other subjects and AMP for math. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
